overview.text: Proteins are large biological molecules built from one or more chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. The order of amino acids helps determine how a chain folds into a distinctive three-dimensional shape, which in turn helps determine what the protein does. Proteins carry out many essential jobs: some speed up chemical reactions as enzymes, while others provide structural support, transport substances, transmit signals, or help defend the body. Proteins also matter in nutrition: foods provide protein that the body uses to build and maintain tissues such as muscles, bones, and skin. Their varied shapes and jobs distinguish proteins from other major biological molecules.

key_facts.text: Amino acids are linked into protein chains by peptide bonds.
The amino-acid sequence helps determine a protein’s three-dimensional shape and specific function.
Protein roles include catalyzing reactions, providing structure, transporting substances, sending signals, and defending against foreign particles.
Proteins in foods help the body build and maintain bones, muscles, and skin.
OpenStax describes 20 common amino acids found in proteins; differences in their side chains give them different chemical properties.
